Turn On, Tune In, Drop Out
TURN ON, TOON IN, DROP OWT
slogan (Boomer slang)
The slogan of Timothy Leary, the former Harvard psychologist turned LSD evangelist, first spoken publicly at a press conference in New York in September 1966 and proclaimed to the crowd at the Human Be-In, San Francisco, January 14, 1967. Leary later said the phrase had been suggested to him by the media theorist Marshall McLuhan. Turn on meant to take psychedelic drugs; tune in, to harmonize with the world around you; drop out, to detach from school, career, and society. Leary insisted he meant the last as self-reliance; the young heard it as quitting.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Turn on, tune in, drop out was the creed of the psychedelic counterculture in six words: take drugs, follow your inner experience, and walk away from school, work, family, and responsibility. Thousands of young people did exactly that. The Christian observation: each of the three verbs has a godly counterpart, and the slogan inverts all of them. To turn on was to chemically alter the mind; Scripture says, "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). To tune in was to follow inner experience; Scripture says to tune in to God’s Word, and warns that "Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom" (Pro 18:1) — the man who withdraws to follow his own desire is the fool of Proverbs, not the sage. To drop out was to abandon work and duty; Scripture says, "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10), and "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). There is a biblical kind of dropping out — "be not conformed to this world" — but it is a departure from sin, not from duty, and it moves the believer toward his neighbor, not away from him. A grandparent who dropped out in 1967 and came back can tell a grandchild the truest version of the slogan: turn to Christ, tune in to His Word, and drop the sin that so easily besets you.

Webster 1828 Definition

Timothy Leary’s psychedelic slogan (1966–67): take drugs, follow inner experience, abandon society — three verbs Scripture inverts: be transformed (Rom 12:2), hear God’s Word, and work heartily as to the Lord (Col 3:23).

expand to see more

TURN ON, TUNE IN, DROP OUT, slogan (Timothy Leary, 1966–67) The counterculture’s call to use psychedelic drugs (turn on), attend to one’s inner experience and surroundings (tune in), and withdraw from conventional society, education, and employment (drop out).

Webster (1828) — TUNE, verb transitive To put into a state adapted to produce the proper sounds; as, to tune a forte-piano; to tune a violin. TUNE your harps. 1. To sing with melody or harmony. Fountains, and ye that warble as ye flow Melodious murmurs, warbling tune his praise. So we say of birds, they tune their notes or lays. 2. To put into a state proper for any purpose, or adapted to produce a particular effect. [ Little Used .]

Decode for families: each verb survives separately — turned on (aroused, excited), tuned in (alert, aware), dropout (one who quits school).

Key Scripture

Rom 12:2 — "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God."

Pro 18:1 — "Through desire a man, having separated himself, seeketh and intermeddleth with all wisdom."

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

1Pe 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

Modern Corruption

Leary’s slogan made drugs the door, the self the guide, and withdrawal the goal; Scripture makes the renewed mind the door, God’s Word the guide, and faithful work the calling.

expand to see more

Leary marketed a religion. He called LSD a sacrament, founded the League for Spiritual Discovery in 1966, and preached a gospel of inner liberation that asked nothing of the convert but a dose. Its fruit was a generation of young people who left school and family to live in crash pads, many of whom never fully returned. The slogan’s genius was that it sounded like spiritual seriousness — tune in, wake up, leave the rat race — while it was really the oldest temptation in the book: separate yourself, follow your desire, and call it wisdom (Pro 18:1).

The gospel also calls men out. But it calls them out of darkness into His marvelous light, out of sin into service, and out of the self into the body of Christ. The Christian does not drop out of his duties; he does them "heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23). He does not turn on with a chemical; he stays "sober" and "vigilant" (1Pe 5:8). And he does not tune in to himself; he tunes in to the voice that says, "This is my beloved Son: hear him."

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Turn on (1960s, to take drugs) + tune in (radio) + drop out (to quit) → Leary’s slogan, September 1966 press conference and January 14, 1967 Human Be-In.

expand to see more

Turn on — 1960s slang: to take a drug; to excite (from switching on a device)

Tune in — from radio: to adjust to a frequency; hence to become attuned

Drop out — to withdraw from school or society; dropout (n.) by 1930

September 1966: Leary’s New York press conference; League for Spiritual Discovery

January 14, 1967: proclaimed at the Human Be-In, San Francisco

Usage

""Grandpa says he turned on, tuned in, and dropped out for about six months, then Grandma made him get a job.""

"If any would not work, neither should he eat (2Th 3:10)."

"Be transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2), not by altering it."
